item.title: He Was Going to Bleed on Me?? College student escaped knife attack and ran for help - then was shot by cops five times
item.description: A college student is suing after cops shot him five times while he tried to flee a hostage situation and knife attack in his own home. Maverick Lyon, 21, was fleeing his family's North Albany, Oregon, home after being held at knifepoint by his brother, John “Dakota” Lyon, 27, when officers opened fire on January 6. The lawsuit against the city and two cops accuses officers of mishandling the response, citing poor communication, a lack of coordination and their failure to use the father's descriptions of the brothers' clothing to distinguish the hostage from the suspected attacker. Lyon repeatedly mouthed “Help me!” through a window as officers approached, but received no response, according to the lawsuit. When he finally ran out the back door with both hands raised, he had already dropped the knife he was carrying in self-defense. Officers Matt Thomas and Engle Diaz opened fire, with Diaz continuing to shoot after Lyon fell, the lawsuit alleges. “You shot the wrong guy – he was holding me hostage,” Lyon told officers as he lay bleeding on the ground, according toRing doorbell camera footage cited in the lawsuit. Lyon was hospitalized for four weeks and underwent several operations, including the removal of part of his lungs, appendix and spleen. The shooting forced him to miss a semester at St. Anselm College in New Hampshire and his senior lacrosse season. He has since returned to playing but will need additional orthopedic and plastic surgery to repair his facial injuries, his attorney Alicia LeDuc Montgomery said. The incident began after Lyon's father called 911 to report that Dakota was holding his younger brother at knifepoint inside their family home. Dakota struggled with drug use following a knee injury and was living in a separate studio apartment inside his parents' home after being released from prison in November 2025. He was serving post-prison supervision for a previous assault and weapons conviction. https://www.the-independent.com/news/world/americas/crime/college-student-shot-by-cops-oregon-b3079885.html

item.description: What was your favorite horror movie to rent at Blockbuster? And secondly, which was your favorite VHS cover to look at while browsing? You can pay $14.99 a month for Amazon Prime and still reach movie night with another rental charge waiting for you. Your membership covers the titles marked “Included with Prime.” The rest can carry a separate price, even when the movie’s been around for decades. That’s part of what makes the idea of a Blockbuster trip feel so appealing. You could make an evening out of choosing: taking your time, considering something unfamiliar, finding a snack to go with it. The anticipation belonged to movie night, too. The supplied listings put a 4K Amazon rental of 1996’s Independence Day at $3.99 and a UHD rental of 1998’s Practical Magic at $5.99. Prime doesn’t promise access to every film in the store, and a title that was included can become a separate purchase when rights arrangements change. There’s only 1 place where the name survives: the independently franchised Blockbuster in Bend, Oregon, the last remaining store since early 2020.

item.title: HIV Used to Be a Death Sentence. Science Had Other Plans.
item.description:
SCIENCE: RUINING DEATH'S PLANS SINCE FOREVER. There was a time when an HIV diagnosis meant preparing for the worst. Not because doctors didn't care. Not because patients weren't fighting. But because medical science simply hadn't caught up with the virus.
Then something extraordinary happened. Scientists did what scientists do. They studied. They experimented. They failed. They tried again. They developed antiretroviral treatments that transformed HIV from an often-fatal diagnosis into a manageable chronic condition for millions of people. Today, with consistent access to effective treatment, people living with HIV can enjoy long, healthy lives. And here's the genuinely remarkable part: U=U. Undetectable equals Untransmittable. Someone living with HIV who maintains an undetectable viral load does not transmit the virus through sex. Think about the enormity of that achievement. A disease that once inspired widespread terror, stigma, and discrimination can now be controlled so effectively that sexual transmission is prevented. Not by wishful thinking. Not by a motivational podcast. Not by some bloke selling miracle supplements between conspiracy theories. By decades of painstaking, evidence-based fucking science. HIV hasn't disappeared. There's still no widely available cure, and millions of people face barriers to lifesaving treatment. But this is what human progress actually looks like. Not a flashy announcement. Not a billionaire promising to revolutionize everything before lunch. Just generations of researchers, healthcare workers, advocates, and patients refusing to accept that things couldn't get better. The virus didn't surrender. Science refused to. ❤️ #HIV #AIDS #Science #MedicalBreakthrough #AntiretroviralTherapy #UequalsU #UndetectableEqualsUntransmittable #PublicHealth #MedicalResearch #ScienceWins #EndTheStigma https://www.who.int/en/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/hiv-aids/?utm_source=chatgpt.com

item.title: My cat had a heart attack.
item.description:
His name was Dyrone, a nickname of a LCS player Dyrus from the 2010s. He loved watching games with us.
He was fluffy and sweet. He loved pets and cuddles. Eternal lap kitty. He forced everyone to pet him.
He loved playing with crinkle toys and hair ties. And being annoying until you paid attention.
He loved naps alone and looked dead every time.
His best angle.
He was 15. He had a heart attack and passed away while we were driving him to the emergency vet. I'm struggling to accept it and I just wanted to share him with people. Show your pets extra love for me and him tonight please.

item.description: In the late 1980s, Nintendo operated a real-life “Game Counselor” hotline that players could call if they got stuck in a game. For a fee, callers could speak directly to trained counselors at Nintendo’s headquarters in Redmond, Washington, who would walk them through difficult levels, hidden secrets, and boss fights over the phone. The service became so popular during the height of the NES era that Nintendo reportedly employed dozens of counselors, many of whom spent their entire workday helping frustrated kids and parents beat games like The Legend of Zelda, Metroid, and Super Mario Bros. 3. This footage, featured in an ABC News segment from the late 1980s, shows one of those counselors taking a live call from a player asking for help getting past a level. Long before YouTube walkthroughs, Google searches, or online forums existed, hotlines like this were one of the only ways gamers could get immediate help without buying a strategy guide. Nintendo also published “Nintendo Power,” a magazine filled with maps, cheat codes, and tips, but for many players, calling the hotline and speaking to a real person felt like having a gaming expert on speed dial...
